questions.title: Reverse A Linked List
questions.summary: Reverse a singly linked list and return the new head.
questions.prompt: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list in place and return the new head node.

examples.explanation: Every next pointer is redirected to the previous node.

constraints: Do not allocate a second list in the iterative solution.

solutionTracks.title: Iterative Pointer Reversal
solutionTracks.summary: Walk the list once while redirecting each node to point at the previous node instead of the next node.

steps.title: Hold previous and current
steps.explanation: Previous starts empty and current starts at the head.

steps.title: Save next before rewiring
steps.explanation: Store current.next before overwriting it so the rest of the list is not lost.

steps.title: Advance both pointers
steps.explanation: Move previous to current and current to the saved next node until the list ends.

solutionTracks.explanation: At every step, previous is the head of the already reversed prefix and current is the first node not yet reversed. Rewiring current extends the reversed prefix by one node.

python.label: Python
python.code:
def reverse_list(head):
    prev = None
    cur = head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = nxt
    return prev

solutionTracks.title: Recursive Reversal
solutionTracks.summary: Let recursion reverse the tail, then attach the current node after its original next node.

steps.title: Find the new head
steps.explanation: When the recursive call reaches the last node, that node becomes the new head.

steps.title: Flip the edge
steps.explanation: After the tail is reversed, current.next.next should point back to current.

steps.title: Break the old edge
steps.explanation: Set current.next to null so the old forward link does not create a cycle.

solutionTracks.explanation: The recursive call returns a fully reversed suffix. Repointing the suffix tail back to the current node adds the current node to the end of that reversed suffix.

python.label: Python
python.code:
def reverse_list_recursive(head):
    if not head or not head.next:
        return head
    new_head = reverse_list_recursive(head.next)
    head.next.next = head
    head.next = None
    return new_head

questions.title: Merge Intervals
questions.summary: Combine overlapping intervals into the smallest set of non-overlapping ranges.
questions.prompt: Given a list of closed intervals, merge every overlapping interval and return the condensed list.

solutionTracks.title: Sort Then Merge
solutionTracks.summary: Sort intervals by start time and extend the current merged interval while overlaps continue.

steps.title: Sort by start
steps.explanation: Once intervals are sorted, any overlap with the current interval must be adjacent in the scan.

steps.title: Compare starts to current end
steps.explanation: If the next start is within the current end, extend the current end to cover both intervals.

steps.title: Start a new group
steps.explanation: If the next start is after the current end, append a new independent interval.

solutionTracks.explanation: Sorting removes the need to compare every interval with every other interval. A future interval can only overlap the active merged interval if its start is within the active end.

solutionTracks.title: Endpoint Sweep
solutionTracks.summary: Convert interval endpoints into events and rebuild merged ranges from transitions between inactive and active coverage.

steps.title: Create events
steps.explanation: Represent each start as plus one active interval and each end as minus one active interval.

steps.title: Sort endpoints
steps.explanation: Process starts before ends at the same coordinate when closed intervals should merge.

steps.title: Record coverage spans
steps.explanation: A merged interval starts when active count rises from zero and ends when it returns to zero.

solutionTracks.explanation: The active count tells whether at least one interval covers the current position. Boundaries where that count changes between zero and nonzero are exactly the merged interval edges.

questions.title: Validate Parentheses Stream
questions.summary: Check whether a stream of delimiters is balanced and properly nested.
questions.prompt: Given a string of bracket characters, return true if every closing bracket matches the latest unmatched opening bracket.

examples.explanation: Every close matches the latest open.

constraints: Input contains only (, ), [, ], {, and }. Both solutions support all three types.

solutionTracks.title: Stack Validation
solutionTracks.summary: Push opening delimiters and require every closing delimiter to match the most recent opening delimiter.

steps.title: Push opens
steps.explanation: Opening brackets create obligations that must be closed in reverse order.

steps.title: Check closes
steps.explanation: A closing bracket is valid only if the stack top is the corresponding opening bracket.

steps.title: Require empty stack
steps.explanation: After reading the stream, all opening obligations must have been closed.

solutionTracks.explanation: Balanced delimiters are last-in first-out. The stack captures that nested structure exactly, so any mismatched or leftover item proves the stream is invalid.

solutionTracks.title: Repeated Adjacent-Pair Removal
solutionTracks.summary: Remove valid neighboring pairs until no change remains.

steps.title: Remove them repeatedly
steps.explanation: Removing an inner valid pair can expose an outer pair.

steps.title: Check the remainder
steps.explanation: Empty means balanced. A nonempty fixed point cannot be a valid bracket string.

solutionTracks.explanation: Every nonempty balanced bracket string has an innermost adjacent pair. Removing that pair preserves validity; repeated removal therefore empties every valid string. Removing valid adjacent pairs cannot repair a mismatched nesting order. Use the linear stack solution under interview time pressure; this baseline is simpler to explain but may scan O(n) times.
